H&P – Super Detailed

Consult Summary:
26-year-old known asthmatic presents with 2–3 day history of worsening exertional dyspnoea, wheeze and dry cough poorly relieved by salbutamol; likely mild asthma exacerbation—plan to step-up inhaled steroid, continue reliever, and arrange urgent face-to-face GP review with safety-netting.

History:
• Presenting complaint: Chest tightness, wheeze, and shortness of breath.  
• Onset/progression: Began 2–3 days ago while running; now occurs with brisk walking. Symptoms persisting, not improving.  
• Relieving factors: Salbutamol inhaler provides minimal relief.  
• Aggravating factors: Physical exertion.  
• Associated symptoms: Dry cough; denies sputum production. No fever, chest pain, haemoptysis, or syncope reported.  
• Review of systems: No additional systemic or ENT symptoms mentioned.

Past Medical History:
• Asthma – generally well-controlled; last attack 3–4 years ago; no prior hospital admissions; never required oral steroids.  
• Hay fever (allergic rhinitis).  
• Possible eczema (self-reported; uses emollient and topical steroid).  

Medications:
• Salbutamol inhaler, dose/route/frequency not documented (used PRN up to daily).  
• Clenil (beclomethasone) inhaler 3 puffs BID (patient); dose verified by clinician.  
• Cetraben cream, dose/route/frequency not documented.  
• Topical hydrocortisone, dose/route/frequency not documented.  

Allergies:
• No known drug allergies.  

Social History:
• Physically active; recreational runner.  
• Smoking: not discussed.  
• Alcohol / other substances: not discussed.  
• Lives at 28 Great Road SW19 1EZ; no other social or occupational factors recorded.  

Family History:
• Brother – asthma.  
• Sister – eczema.  

Physical Examination:
(No physical examination performed during video consult.)

Investigations:
• Home peak-flow when well: ~380 L/min (patient-reported).  
• No current peak-flow, vitals, imaging, or labs available.

Assessment & Plan:
Issue 1: Suspected mild asthma exacerbation / loss of control  
— Assessment: 2–3 day increase in wheeze, SOB; poor response to reliever; possible trigger exercise/allergen; no red-flag features yet.  
— Plan:  
  • Increase Clenil to 4 puffs BID until reviewed.  
  • Continue salbutamol up to every 2 hours PRN; advise that frequent use indicates poor control.  
  • Arrange urgent face-to-face GP appointment within few days for chest exam, inhaler technique check, and peak-flow measurement.  
  • Provide safety-net: If breathlessness worsens or salbutamol required more frequently without relief, attend Emergency Department immediately.  
  • Possible need for oral steroids and/or antibiotics to be decided at review.

Issue 2: Routine asthma management  
— Assessment: Last formal asthma review 2 years ago; no recent action plan.  
— Plan:  
  • Schedule comprehensive asthma review with practice nurse (spirometry, action plan, vaccinations).  
  • Reinforce daily preventer adherence and correct inhaler technique at review.

Issue 3: Atopic conditions (hay fever / possible eczema)  
— Assessment: Background allergic rhinitis and skin symptoms.  
— Plan: Monitor; no acute intervention required today.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx):
1. Asthma exacerbation – High likelihood; fits known asthma, acute increase in wheeze/SOB, minimal reliever response.  
2. Viral URTI triggering asthma – Moderate likelihood; common precipitant though absent typical viral symptoms.  
3. Exercise-induced bronchoconstriction / poor inhaler technique – Moderate likelihood as initial trigger; persistence suggests broader loss of control.

Quality checks (document_quality):
• Expected but missing: vital signs, current peak-flow, full allergy list, smoking/alcohol history, comprehensive medication doses.  
• Conflicts: Patient first mentioned “Flanel Bactroban” vs later clarified “Cetraben” (possible transcription error).  
• Transcript quality: Clear overall, occasional audio garble leading to minor medication name uncertainty.
